q: What is the time complexity of count_halvings(n)?
code:
def count_halvings(n):
    steps = 0
    while n > 1:
        n = n // 2
        steps += 1
    return steps

print(count_halvings(1_000_000))
options: O(n): the loop runs once for each value from n down to 1
O(log n): it counts how many times n can be halved
O(n / 2): halving cuts the work in half
O(sqrt(n)): the value shrinks faster than linearly
why: The loop runs as many times as n can be halved before reaching 1, which is about log2(n). That is why one million takes only 19 steps, and doubling n adds just one more step.
wrong: n drops by half each step, not by 1, so most values are skipped. For n = 1,000,000 it prints only 19.
Halving the value each step is not the same as doing half the steps. And O(n / 2) would just be O(n).
Square root growth comes from loops like while i * i <= n. Repeated halving gives a logarithm, which is far smaller.

q: countPairs compares every pair of positions once. The inner loop starts at i + 1, so it gets shorter each time. What is the time complexity?
options: O(n log n), because the inner loop keeps shrinking
O(n), because each pair is checked only once
O(n^2 / 2), which is a smaller class than O(n^2)
O(n^2): the comparisons add up to about n^2 / 2
why: The inner loop runs n - 1, n - 2, ..., 1, 0 times, which adds up to n(n - 1) / 2. Constant factors are dropped, so this is O(n^2). Starting j at i + 1 halves the work but does not change the growth rate.
wrong: The inner loop shrinks by one each time, not by half. The total is n(n - 1) / 2 comparisons, which is quadratic.
There are about n^2 / 2 pairs, so checking each pair once is still quadratic work.
Big-O drops constant factors. n^2 / 2 and n^2 are the same class.

q: A function makes one pass over n numbers to find the maximum, then a second, separate pass to count how often that maximum appears. What is its time complexity?
options: O(n): the two passes add up to 2n steps
O(n^2), because there are two loops
O(2n), which grows faster than O(n)
O(n log n), because the second pass depends on the first
why: Sequential loops add: n + n = 2n steps, and the constant 2 is dropped. Loops only multiply when one runs inside the other.
wrong: The loops run one after the other, not one inside the other. Their costs add (n + n), they do not multiply.
2n is n times a constant, and Big-O drops constants. Two passes are still linear.
Using a result from the first pass does not add a log factor. Each pass is a plain linear scan.

q: For each of n user names, code loops over a blocklist of m names that grows over time and compares them. A reviewer calls it O(n^2). What is the most accurate bound?
options: O(n + m)
O(n * m)
O(n)
why: Each of the n names is compared with each of the m blocked names, so there are n * m comparisons. Keep separate letters for inputs of different sizes. Putting the blocklist in a set would bring it down to O(n + m).
wrong: That treats both inputs as the same size. With 1,000,000 users and 10 blocked names, the real work is far below n^2.
The loops are nested: every user is compared with every blocked name, so the costs multiply.
The blocklist grows, so its size is an input. Dropping m hides real cost as the list gets longer.

q: Version A scans a list twice. Version B does the same work in a single pass. A teammate says A is O(2n), a worse complexity class than B. What is right?
options: A is right: O(2n) is a worse class than O(n)
Neither: Big-O cannot compare two versions of the same code
Both are O(n); B can still be faster in practice
Both are O(1), since the number of passes is fixed
why: Big-O describes how cost grows, and constant factors are dropped, so 2n and n are both O(n). Constants still matter on a real machine, which is why B can be faster with the same Big-O.
wrong: Big-O ignores constant factors, so O(2n) and O(n) name the same class.
Big-O can compare any two algorithms by how they grow. Here both grow linearly.
The number of passes is fixed, but each pass still grows with n, so the total is linear.

q: One textbook writes binary search as O(log2 n), another as O(log10 n), and many just write O(log n). Why is that fine?
options: Logs of different bases differ only by a constant factor
Because n is always a power of 2 in practice
It is not fine: O(log2 n) grows faster, so it is a different class
Because logarithms grow so slowly that they count as O(1)
why: log2 n = log10 n / log10 2, so switching bases multiplies by a fixed number (about 3.32). Big-O drops constant factors, so every base gives the same class.
wrong: n can be any size. The base does not matter for any n, power of 2 or not.
log2 n is about 3.32 times log10 n for every n. A fixed multiplier never changes the class.
log n keeps growing with n, slowly but without limit, so it is not constant.

q: repeatX builds a string of n characters in a loop. Java strings are immutable. What is the time complexity?
options: O(n): one short append per iteration
O(n log n): the string grows like a dynamic array
O(n), since each new string reuses the old one's memory
O(n^2): each += copies the whole string so far
why: Because a String cannot change, s += "x" makes a new string and copies the old one into it. The copies cost 1 + 2 + ... + n, which is O(n^2): doubling n roughly quadruples the time. A StringBuilder makes the loop O(n).
wrong: Each += creates a new string and copies every character so far: 1 + 2 + ... + n copies.
That is how StringBuilder grows. A String cannot grow in place; every += copies the whole thing.
Immutable strings cannot be extended in place, so the old characters are copied every time.

q: reversed_copy builds the reversed list by inserting each item at the front. For a list of n items, what is the time complexity?
options: O(n): there is exactly one insert per item
O(n^2): each insert(0, x) shifts the items already in out
O(n log n): each insert into a list costs O(log n)
O(n): Python lists are linked lists, so front inserts are cheap
why: A Python list stores items in one contiguous array, so inserting at index 0 shifts all current items: 0 + 1 + ... + (n - 1) moves, O(n^2). Appending and then calling reverse(), or a deque with appendleft, makes it O(n).
wrong: insert(0, x) is not O(1) on a Python list. It moves every existing element one slot to the right.
That is a balanced search tree. A Python list is an array, so inserting at the front costs O(length).
Python lists are dynamic arrays. A collections.deque would make front inserts O(1).

q: unique keeps the first copy of each item. For n mostly distinct items, what is its time complexity, and what is the simplest fix?
options: O(n^2): x not in seen scans a list; a set makes it O(n)
O(n): it is a single loop over the items
O(n log n): Python searches lists with binary search
O(n^2), and no fix exists: removing duplicates must compare all pairs
why: The loop runs n times, and each in on a list is a linear scan, so mostly distinct items give O(n^2). A set checks membership by hash in O(1) on average, so the same loop becomes O(n), and result still keeps the order.
wrong: The loop is single, but x not in seen scans the whole list each time, which is O(n) per check.
in checks a list one element at a time. Binary search needs sorted data and is not what in does.
A set answers membership in O(1) on average, so each item needs only one check.

q: Linear search finds the target at index 0 in some runs. A classmate concludes that linear search is O(1). What is wrong with that reasoning?
options: Nothing: Big-O always describes the best case an algorithm can reach
Linear search is O(log n) on average
That is only the best case; the worst case still checks all n items
Big-O only applies to sorted inputs
why: Best, average and worst case are separate questions. The best case of linear search is 1 check, but the average and worst cases grow with n, so linear search is O(n) in the usual worst-case sense.
wrong: Big-O is a bound you state for a chosen case. Unqualified, interview answers usually mean the worst case.
With no order to exploit, the target is on average about halfway in: n / 2 checks, which is O(n).
Big-O applies to any algorithm and input. Sortedness only decides which algorithms are possible.

q: A problem says n can be up to 100,000 and the time limit is about one second. Which complexity should you aim for?
options: O(n^2) is fine, since computers do billions of steps a second
O(n log n) or better: about 1.7 million steps
O(2^n), as long as the code is well optimized
Any complexity, since the limit on n is only about memory
why: A typical judge manages roughly 10^8 simple steps per second. n log n at n = 100,000 is about 1.7 million steps, while n^2 is 10 billion. The constraint is telling you to avoid quadratic work.
wrong: n^2 is 10^10 steps here. Even at a billion simple steps a second that is many seconds.
2^100000 is astronomically large; no optimization rescues an exponential algorithm at this size.
The limit on n is the main hint about the time complexity the problem expects.

q: This recursive binary search is correct, but it slices the list on each call. On a sorted list of n items, what is its worst-case time?
options: O(log n): the list is halved on every call
O(n log n): each of the log n calls copies n items
O(n^2): slicing copies the whole list on every single call
O(n): the copies add up to n/2 + n/4 + ..., about n
why: There are about log n calls, but arr[mid + 1:] and arr[:mid] build new lists. The copies cost n/2 + n/4 + ... < n, so the total is O(n), no better than a linear scan. Passing lo and hi indices instead keeps it O(log n).
wrong: The number of calls is O(log n), but each slice copies half the remaining items, and those copies dominate.
Each call copies only the remaining half, not the full list, so the copies form a shrinking series that sums to about n.
A slice copies only the part it takes. The parts halve each time, so the total stays linear.

q: Algorithm A is O(n) but does heavy work per item. Algorithm B is O(n log n) with very light steps. For n = 50, which statement is right?
options: A is always faster, because O(n) beats O(n log n) at every size
Big-O gives exact times, so just compare 50 with 50 log 50
B is faster for every n, since its steps are lighter
B may well be faster; A is only sure to win at large n
why: Big-O describes growth and drops constant factors. An O(n) algorithm with a big constant can lose to an O(n log n) one at small n; it is only guaranteed to win beyond some size. When n is small, measure.
wrong: Big-O hides constant factors. At small n a large constant can outweigh the extra log factor.
Big-O drops constants and lower terms, so it cannot give actual times. Measure instead.
Light steps help at small n, but n log n grows faster, so A wins once n is large enough.

q: longest_run returns the length of the longest block of equal neighbours. It has a while loop inside a while loop. What is its time complexity?
code:
def longest_run(a):
    best = 0
    i = 0
    while i < len(a):
        j = i
        while j < len(a) and a[j] == a[i]:
            j += 1
        best = max(best, j - i)
        i = j
    return best

print(longest_run([1, 1, 2, 2, 2, 3]))
options: O(n^2): a loop inside a loop is quadratic
O(n): j never moves back, and i jumps to j
O(n^2) in the worst case, when every item is equal
O(n log n): the inner loop skips over blocks of items
why: j only moves forward, and i = j resumes where the inner loop stopped, so over the whole run the inner loop steps through each index once. Total work is O(n). The same reasoning makes two pointer and sliding window code linear.
wrong: Nesting alone does not decide it. Count total steps: j only moves forward, and i jumps to where j stopped.
When all items are equal, the inner loop runs n times once and then i jumps to the end. That is O(n).
Skipping blocks is not halving anything. The work is simply proportional to n.

q: factorial has a base case for n == 1. What happens when this runs?
options: 120, then 1
120, then 0
120, then a RecursionError
A RecursionError before anything is printed
why: factorial(0) skips the base case and calls factorial(-1), which keeps going down and never reaches 1. Python stops it at the recursion limit with RecursionError. A base case of n <= 1 fixes it: the base case must be reachable from every valid input.
wrong: There is no case for 0, so factorial(0) never returns 1; it calls factorial(-1), factorial(-2), and so on.
Nothing here returns 0. The calls go down forever, past 0, until the stack limit.
factorial(5) does reach n == 1, so 120 is printed first.

q: total adds up a list recursively, and its base case is correct. What happens when this runs with Python's default settings?
options: 4950, then a RecursionError for the 100,000 item list
4950, then a MemoryError, because the list itself is too large
A RecursionError on the first call, because i=0 is a shared default
why: Recursion depth equals the list length, and every pending call keeps a stack frame. CPython limits the depth to about 1000 by default, so 100,000 levels raise RecursionError. A loop, or sum(items), has no such limit.
wrong: The logic is right, but each item adds a stack frame, and 100,000 frames exceed Python's default limit of about 1000.
A list of 100,000 ints is small. The limit hit is the call depth, not the data size.
An int default is immutable, so sharing it is harmless. The first call works and prints 4950.

q: A recursive function on n items creates no lists, dicts or other data structures, and it calls itself n levels deep. How much extra space does it use?
options: O(1), because it allocates no lists or other data structures
O(n), for the stack frames of the n pending calls
O(log n), because the frames are reused
O(n^2), because each frame copies the data
why: Each call waits for the one below it, so at the deepest point n frames sit on the stack at once. Space analysis counts this stack, which is why recursion n levels deep uses O(n) extra space even without data structures.
wrong: Every pending call keeps a frame with its arguments and return address on the call stack. Those frames are memory.
A frame cannot be reused while its call is still waiting for the one below. At depth n, n frames exist at once.
Passing a list passes a reference, so no copy is made. Only the frames themselves add up.

q: This naive fib counts its own calls; for fib(25) it prints 242785. How does the number of calls grow with n?
options: Linearly: one call per value from n down to 0
Quadratically: about n^2 calls
Logarithmically: the problem shrinks on every call
Exponentially: about 1.6 times more per step
why: fib(n) calls fib(n - 1) and fib(n - 2), and no result is saved, so the same values are recomputed again and again. The call count grows about 1.6 times per step (fib(26) makes 392,835 calls): exponential time, while the stack depth is only n.
wrong: Each call makes two more, and the same values are recomputed many times, so there are far more calls than n.
25^2 is only 625, but the count is 242,785. The count multiplies with each step instead of adding.
n shrinks by only 1 or 2 per call, not by half, and each call branches in two.

q: To avoid a stack overflow on deep input, a Java developer rewrites a recursive method so that the recursive call is the very last thing it does. Does that help?
options: No: Java still uses one frame per call; a loop is the fix
Yes: a tail call always reuses the caller's stack frame, in any language
Yes, but only if the method is also static
No, because tail recursion makes the running time exponential
why: Tail call elimination is a compiler or runtime feature. The standard JVM does not do it, and neither does CPython, so a tail-recursive method still uses one frame per level. Rewriting it as a loop is the reliable fix.
wrong: Some languages guarantee that (Scheme, for one), but Java and Python do not. Every call still pushes a frame.
static does not matter here. The JVM does no tail call elimination either way.
Moving the call to the end does not change how many calls are made. The only issue is stack depth.

q: You need to list every file in a folder, including all nested subfolders. Folders are rarely more than 20 levels deep. Why is recursion a natural fit here?
options: Recursion is always faster than the equivalent loop would be
Recursion uses less memory than a loop
A folder holds folders, so the code mirrors the data
A loop cannot visit nested folders at all
why: A folder tree is defined in terms of itself, so "handle this folder, then each subfolder the same way" is short and clear. The small depth keeps the stack safe. For very deep data, a loop with an explicit stack avoids overflow.
wrong: Recursion adds call overhead. It is chosen for clarity on recursive data, not for speed.
Each level adds a stack frame, so recursion usually uses more memory. That is fine here only because the depth is small.
A loop with an explicit stack or queue can visit them too. Recursion is just the simpler way to write it.

q: sumTo has a base case for 0, and each call lowers n by 2. What happens when main runs?
options: 6, then 9
Compile error: sumTo might not return a value
6, then a StackOverflowError
6, then the program hangs forever with no error
why: sumTo(4) goes 4, 2, 0 and returns 6. sumTo(5) goes 5, 3, 1, -1 and never equals 0, so frames pile up until the JVM throws StackOverflowError. A base case must be reachable: if (n <= 0) would fix it.
wrong: From 5 the values are 5, 3, 1, -1, ...: they jump over 0, so the base case is never hit.
Every path ends in a return statement, so it compiles.
Each call adds a stack frame, so it does not run forever; it fails as soon as the stack is full.

q: show prints after its recursive call returns. What does show(3) print?
why: show(3) calls show(2), which calls show(1), which calls show(0), and that returns at once. The prints then run as the calls unwind: 1, then 2, then 3. Code after a recursive call runs in reverse order of the calls.
wrong: That would happen if print came before the recursive call. Here each call waits for show(n - 1) to finish first.
Every call that is not the base case prints once, so three numbers appear.
show(0) returns at the base case without printing.

q: Orders are already listed by time. You sort them by customer name with a stable sort. What does stability guarantee?
options: The sort never crashes, even on huge inputs
The same input always gives the same output
It runs in O(n log n) time even in the worst case
Orders of the same customer stay in time order
why: A stable sort keeps items with equal keys in the order they had before. The orders were by time, so each customer's orders stay in time order. This is what makes sorting in several passes work.
wrong: Stability is not about robustness. It is only about the relative order of items with equal keys.
Unstable sorts are usually deterministic too. Stability is about equal keys keeping their original order.
Stability and speed are separate properties. Insertion sort is stable and O(n^2).

q: Python's sort is stable. The list is sorted by day, then sorted again by name. What does it print?
code:
# each order is (customer, day)
orders = [("bob", 3), ("amy", 2), ("bob", 1), ("amy", 1)]
orders.sort(key=lambda o: o[1])   # by day
orders.sort(key=lambda o: o[0])   # then by name
print(orders)
options: The days within each name come out in random order
why: The last sort sets the primary order, by name. For equal names a stable sort keeps the order from before, which the first sort made by day. So sorting by the secondary key first and the primary key last gives name, then day.
wrong: That is the original order within each name, as if the first sort never happened. Stability keeps the day order from the first sort.
That is the result of the first sort only. The last sort decides the main order, so names come first.
The last sort ignores days as a key, but a stable sort keeps equal names in their current order, which is already by day.

q: A quicksort always picks the first element as the pivot. What happens when it is given an array that is already sorted?
options: It slows to O(n^2): one side of every split is empty
It finishes in O(n), since there is nothing left to move
It stays O(n log n), as quicksort always is
It fails, since a sorted array has no valid pivot
why: On sorted input the first element is the smallest, so each partition puts nothing on the left and everything else on the right. That gives n levels of up to n work each, O(n^2), and n levels of recursion. A random pivot avoids it in practice.
wrong: Quicksort still partitions at every level; sorted input does not let it skip that work.
O(n log n) is quicksort's average case. With bad pivots it is O(n^2).
Any element can be a pivot. The problem is that the smallest one makes very unbalanced splits.

q: You must sort a huge array on a device with almost no spare memory, and a slow worst case is not acceptable. Which algorithm meets both needs?
options: Merge sort: O(n log n) on every input, best and worst
Quicksort: in-place and fast on average
Heap sort: O(n log n) worst case and in-place
Insertion sort: in-place and simple
why: Heap sort builds a heap inside the array itself and repeatedly moves the largest item to the end. It uses O(1) extra memory and O(n log n) time even in the worst case. It is not stable, but stability was not required.
wrong: Merge sort on an array needs an O(n) buffer for merging, which this device does not have.
Its worst case is O(n^2) with bad pivots, which the requirement rules out.
It is in-place, but O(n^2) on general input, far too slow for a huge array.

q: You must sort 10 million ages, each a whole number from 0 to 120. Why can this be done in O(n), below the usual O(n log n) for sorting?
options: The n log n bound no longer holds on modern CPUs
Counting sort tallies each age without comparing items
Ages are small numbers, so comparing them is free
Any sort is O(n) when the data holds many duplicate values
why: The n log n lower bound applies only to sorts that learn the order by comparing pairs. Counting sort uses the small key range instead: 121 counters, one pass to count, one pass to write out. That is O(n + k) with k = 121.
wrong: The bound is a math fact about comparison sorts, and it holds on any hardware.
Cheap comparisons still need about n log n of them. The trick is to avoid comparisons altogether.
Not any sort: merge sort still does about n log n work here. Linear time comes from using the small key range directly.

q: A classmate claims a general sort that learns the order only by comparing pairs of elements, and runs in O(n) in the worst case. What should you say?
options: Plausible: radix sort already sorts in linear time like that
Plausible, as long as it is written in a fast compiled language
Impossible, but only because no sort of any kind can beat O(n^2)
Impossible: comparison sorts need about n log n comparisons
why: n items can be in n factorial different orders, and each yes or no comparison can at best halve the possibilities left. Telling them all apart takes about log2 of n factorial comparisons, which is about n log n. So O(n) worst case is out of reach.
wrong: Radix sort does not compare elements; it reads their digits. So it does not fit the claim.
The bound counts comparisons, not seconds. No language lowers the number of comparisons needed.
Merge sort and heap sort are O(n log n) in the worst case, well below n^2.

q: A list of 100,000 items is already sorted except for a few items that are slightly out of place. Why can insertion sort be a good choice here?
options: It is O(n log n) in the worst case, like merge sort
It uses binary search, so each insert is O(log n)
It is a poor choice: insertion sort is always O(n^2) time
Items move only a few slots, so it runs in about O(n)
why: Insertion sort's work grows with the number of out-of-order pairs. When almost everything is in place, each item is compared once or twice and barely moves, so the total is close to O(n). This is why real sort libraries use it for small or nearly sorted runs.
wrong: Its worst case is O(n^2). Its strength is that its cost depends on how unsorted the input is.
Plain insertion sort shifts items one slot at a time. The speed here comes from short shifts, not search.
O(n^2) is the worst case. On nearly sorted input the inner loop stops almost at once.

q: rank sorts the list it receives. What does this print?
why: list.sort() sorts in place: it rearranges the existing list and returns None, a signal that no new list was made. data and scores are the same list, so data is now sorted. Use sorted(...) when you want a new list.
wrong: list.sort() does not make a sorted copy; that is what sorted(scores) does.
sort() changes the list in place and returns None, so result is None.
The function received a reference to the same list, so sorting scores also sorts data.

q: Why is merge sort O(n log n)?
options: About log n levels of halving, each with O(n) merge work
Each of the n items is compared with log n others in one pass
It runs a binary search for each of the n items
Merging two halves costs log n, and there are n merges
why: Splitting in half again and again gives about log2(n) levels. At each level the merges together touch every item once, so each level costs O(n). n work per level times log n levels is O(n log n), in every case.
wrong: Merging works level by level; there is no single pass that does log n comparisons per item.
Merge sort never binary searches. The log n comes from the number of halving levels.
Merging two halves of total size k costs O(k), not log n. Per level, the merges cover all n items.

q: A standard binary search is run on the unsorted array [7, 1, 9, 3, 5] to look for 1. What happens?
options: It still finds 1, just more slowly than on sorted data
It can miss 1, by discarding the half that holds it
It raises an error, because the input is unsorted
It sorts the array first, then searches
why: The middle is 9, and since 1 < 9 it keeps only the left part, [7, 1]. Then it checks 7, and since 1 < 7 it discards 7 and everything after it, so it reports not found. Binary search is only correct on sorted data.
wrong: Binary search discards half the array on each step based on order. Without order it can discard the half that holds the target.
Binary search does not check sortedness; checking would cost O(n). It just gives wrong answers.
It never reorders the input. Sorting is your job before calling it.

q: firstAtLeast should return the index of the first element >= target. It is called with [1, 3, 5, 7] and target 4. What happens?
options: It returns 2, the index of 5
It returns 1, the index of 3
It throws ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException, since hi starts at a.length
It loops forever once lo = 1 and hi = 2
why: With lo = 1 and hi = 2, mid = 1 and a[1] = 3 < 4, so lo = mid sets lo to 1 again. Nothing changes, forever. Every step must shrink the range: lo = mid + 1 fixes it, and the method returns 2.
wrong: That is the intended answer, but the loop gets stuck before it gets there.
The loop never ends, so nothing is returned. And a[1] = 3 is below the target anyway.
mid is always below hi, so a[a.length] is never read.

q: In Java, a binary search keeps lo and hi as ints that can reach about 2 billion. Why is mid = lo + (hi - lo) / 2 preferred over (lo + hi) / 2?
options: lo + hi can overflow int and turn negative
It rounds toward the true middle more accurately
It is faster, since subtraction is cheaper than addition
(lo + hi) / 2 can skip the target when the range is odd
why: A Java int tops out at about 2.147 billion. With lo = 1.5 billion and hi = 2 billion, lo + hi wraps around and (lo + hi) / 2 is -397483648. hi - lo never leaves the range, so lo + (hi - lo) / 2 is always safe.
wrong: Both give the same value whenever there is no overflow. Overflow is the only difference.
The speed is about the same. The reason is correctness for large values.
Both round down the same way, so neither skips elements. Only lo + hi can leave the int range.

q: Packages (n of them, total weight S) must ship in order within D days. You binary search the ship capacity, testing each guess with one O(n) pass. Why is that valid, and what does it cost?
options: The weights are sorted, so it costs O(log n)
If capacity c works, any larger c works too; O(n log n)
If capacity c works, any larger c works too; O(n log S)
It is not valid: binary search needs a sorted array in memory
why: Feasibility is monotonic: small capacities fail, and once one succeeds, all larger ones do. So you can binary search for the smallest that succeeds, about log S guesses, each checked by one O(n) pass: O(n log S) in total.
wrong: The weights need not be sorted. The search is over capacities, and each guess costs an O(n) check.
The log comes from the range of capacities, up to S, not from the number of packages.
Any yes or no test that flips once over a range can be binary searched. No array is needed.

q: A sorted singly linked list has n nodes. Why does binary search not give O(log n) here?
options: It does give O(log n), since the data is sorted
Binary search needs unique values, and the list may hold duplicates
Reaching the middle node takes O(n) steps, so it costs O(n) overall
It is O(n log n): log n steps, each walking n nodes from the head
why: Binary search assumes jumping to the middle is O(1), as with an array index. On a linked list you must walk node by node: n/2, then n/4, and so on, about n steps in total. A plain linear scan is just as fast and simpler.
wrong: Sorted is not enough. Binary search also needs O(1) access to the middle, which a linked list lacks.
Arrays can hold duplicates too, and binary search copes. The problem is reaching the middle.
Each step walks only through the remaining half: n/2 + n/4 + ... is about n, so the total is O(n).

q: A sorted array holds 1,000,000 numbers. At most about how many comparisons does binary search need to find a value or report that it is missing?
options: About 20
About 1,000
About 500,000
why: Each comparison halves the remaining range. 2^20 is 1,048,576, so after about 20 halvings one candidate is left. Doubling the array adds just one more comparison.
wrong: That is the square root of a million. Binary search halves the range, so the count is log2 of n.
That is the average for linear search. Binary search discards half the range on every step.
That is the worst case of linear search, which checks every element.

q: find_first should return the index of the first 2. What does it print?
why: The first mid is 2, and a[2] == 2, so it returns 2 at once. To find the first occurrence, record mid as a candidate and keep searching left with hi = mid - 1 until the range is empty.
wrong: 0 is the right answer, but the code returns as soon as it hits any 2, and the first one it hits is in the middle.
The first mid is (0 + 4) // 2 = 2, and a[2] already matches.
The value is present, and the very first mid lands on it.

q: In a grid maze, each move goes to a neighbouring open cell. You need the fewest moves from the start to the exit. Which search fits?
options: DFS, because it heads deep toward the exit quickly
BFS, because it reaches cells in order of distance
Either one: both always find the shortest path
Neither: shortest paths always need Dijkstra's algorithm
why: BFS explores all cells 1 move away, then 2, then 3, using a queue. The first time it reaches the exit, no shorter route exists. This holds whenever every edge has the same cost.
wrong: DFS finds a path, but the first path it finds can be long and winding. It does not explore by distance.
Only BFS guarantees it on an unweighted graph. DFS may return a much longer path first.
Dijkstra's algorithm is for weighted edges. When every move costs 1, plain BFS finds the shortest path and is simpler.

q: On a road map, roads take different times to drive. Will BFS from your town find the fastest route to another town?
options: No: BFS minimizes the number of roads, not the total time
Yes: BFS always finds shortest paths
Yes, if each town's roads are added fastest first
No: no algorithm can find shortest paths when edges have weights
why: BFS treats every edge as length 1, so it finds the route with the fewest roads. With different travel times you need an algorithm that compares total cost, such as Dijkstra's with a priority queue.
wrong: Only when every edge costs the same. Two slow roads can take longer than three fast ones.
BFS still finishes level by level, so it never compares total times; a route with more but faster roads still loses.
Dijkstra's algorithm does exactly that for non-negative weights.

q: This DFS has no visited set. What happens when it runs?
options: It prints A B C and stops
It prints A B C A and stops
It prints A B C over and over until a RecursionError
Nothing: Python detects the cycle and raises an error at once
why: The graph has the cycle A, B, C, A, and dfs keeps no visited set, so it walks the loop again and again, one stack frame per step, until Python's recursion limit stops it. A visited set, checked before each call, fixes it.
wrong: C links back to A, and nothing records that A was seen, so the search continues.
Nothing stops the walk when A appears again; it repeats B and C, and so on.
Python does not look for cycles. It runs until the call depth hits the recursion limit.

q: A BFS marks a node visited, and records its distance, only when the node is taken out of the queue; nodes already visited are skipped. What is the effect?
options: The distances it reports come out wrong for some nodes
Same distances, but a node can be queued many times
It loops forever on any graph that contains a cycle
No effect at all on time or memory
why: Marking on enqueue puts each node in the queue once. Marking on dequeue still handles each node once at its correct distance, but in dense graphs the same node can be enqueued by many neighbours first, which wastes memory and time.
wrong: The first time a node leaves the queue is still at its shortest distance, since the queue is in distance order.
Visited nodes are skipped when they leave the queue, so cycles are cut. It only does extra work first.
Many neighbours can add the same unvisited node before it leaves the queue, so the queue can fill with duplicates.

q: A tree is very wide but shallow: every node has 1,000 children and the depth is 3. Which search uses far less memory to visit every node?
options: BFS: it never revisits nodes
Both use the same memory, since both visit every node
BFS: a queue takes less memory than a stack
DFS: it holds about one path, not a whole level
why: BFS keeps the whole next level in its queue, and the last level here has 1000^3 nodes. DFS goes down one branch at a time, holding a path of depth 3 plus the siblings still to visit, a few thousand items. For deep, narrow graphs the picture flips.
wrong: Neither revisits nodes in a tree. BFS must hold a whole level, up to a billion nodes here.
They visit the same nodes in similar time, but what they keep in memory at once differs widely.
Queues and stacks cost about the same per item. What differs is how many items each holds at once.

q: On an unweighted graph, your DFS found a path from A to B with 7 edges. What can you conclude about the shortest path?
options: It has exactly 7 edges, since DFS finds the shortest path
It has at least 7 edges
Nothing at all: the path DFS found might not be a real path
It has at most 7 edges, but it may be shorter
why: Any path found gives an upper bound: the shortest is no longer than 7. DFS does not explore by distance, so a shorter path may exist. Use BFS when you need the fewest edges.
wrong: DFS returns the first path it reaches by going deep; a shorter one may sit in a branch it tried later.
A found path is an upper bound, not a lower bound. Shorter routes can exist.
DFS only follows real edges, so the path is valid. It is just not necessarily the shortest.

q: BFS runs on a graph with V vertices and E edges, stored as adjacency lists, with a visited set. What is its time complexity?
options: O(V * E)
O(V + E)
O(E log V)
why: Each vertex enters the queue once thanks to the visited set, and each adjacency list is read once when its vertex is dequeued. Together the lists hold E entries (2E if undirected), so the total is O(V + E).
wrong: Edges are not rescanned for every vertex. Each vertex's list is read once, when that vertex leaves the queue.
That is the cost with an adjacency matrix, where each row has V entries. Lists hold only the real edges.
The log factor comes from a priority queue, as in Dijkstra's algorithm. BFS uses a plain queue with O(1) operations.

q: In an R x C grid with walls and k hospitals, you need every open cell's distance to its nearest hospital. What is the best plan?
options: One BFS from each hospital, keeping the minimum: O(R * C)
DFS from each cell until it reaches a hospital, then keep the result
One BFS that starts with all k hospitals in the queue: O(R * C)
Sort the hospitals by position, then binary search per cell
why: Putting every hospital in the queue at distance 0 makes BFS grow from all of them at once, level by level. Each cell is first reached from its nearest hospital and is visited once, so the whole grid costs O(R * C) whatever k is.
wrong: That is k separate searches, O(k * R * C) in total, which is slow when k is large.
DFS does not find shortest paths, and starting one from every cell repeats work heavily.
With walls, distance is not ordered by position, so there is nothing to binary search.

q: Memoization turns naive recursive Fibonacci from exponential into linear time. Why does adding a cache to merge sort give no such gain?
options: Its halves never overlap, so no result is reused
Merge sort is already O(n), so a cache has nothing to save
Caches only work for numbers, not for arrays
Merge sort is not recursive, so it has no subproblems
why: Memoization pays off only when the same subproblem comes up again and again, as fib(n - 2) does in Fibonacci. Merge sort splits into disjoint halves, so each subarray is sorted exactly once: divide and conquer without overlap.
wrong: Merge sort is O(n log n). The cache fails because no subarray is ever sorted twice.
Any repeated input can be cached. The point is that merge sort never repeats one.
Merge sort is a classic recursive algorithm. Its subproblems exist; they just never repeat.

q: fib now saves each result in memo before returning it. How does its running time grow with n?
options: Still exponentially, since it is still recursive
Linearly, O(n): each value is computed once
Logarithmically, O(log n)
Constant, O(1), since results come from the dictionary
why: Each fib(k) is computed once and stored, and every later request is a dictionary lookup. That is about 2n calls in total, so the time is O(n): it prints 832040 59 for n = 30, and n = 100 makes 199 calls.
wrong: Recursion is not the cost. The cost was recomputing values, and with the memo each fib(k) is computed once.
Every value from n down to 0 is computed once, so the work is about n steps, not log n.
Only repeat calls hit the dictionary. The first call still has to compute all n values.

q: A memoized recursive DP is correct, but for n = 100,000 it crashes in Python with RecursionError. What is the usual fix?
options: Use a larger cache so that more results are kept in memory
Remove the cache, so that each call keeps a smaller stack frame
Use a dict instead of a list for the cache
Rewrite it bottom-up with a loop that fills a table
why: Tabulation computes states in dependency order with a loop, so there is no call stack to overflow. Memoization is often easier to write, but its depth can reach the number of states. Raising the recursion limit is a fragile workaround.
wrong: The cache is not the problem; the call depth is. A larger cache leaves the recursion just as deep.
Without the cache it becomes exponential, and the depth is still about n.
The type of container does not change the recursion depth.

q: Coins are worth 1, 3 and 4. To make 6, a greedy method always takes the largest coin that fits. What does it return, and is it optimal?
options: 4 + 1 + 1, three coins; 3 + 3 needs two
3 + 3, two coins, which is optimal
4 + 1 + 1, three coins, and that is optimal
It fails to make 6 at all
why: Taking the largest coin first looks best locally but leaves 2, which needs two 1s. Greedy only works for some coin systems, such as 1, 5, 10, 25. In general, coin change needs DP over the amounts.
wrong: Greedy takes 4 first, since it is the largest coin that fits, and then needs 1 + 1.
3 + 3 makes 6 with two coins, so greedy's answer is not the best.
There is a 1 coin, so greedy can always finish; it just uses too many coins.

q: You want to fit as many non-overlapping meetings as possible into one room. Which greedy rule gives an optimal answer?
options: Pick the meeting that starts earliest, then repeat
Pick the shortest meeting, then repeat
Pick the meeting that ends earliest, then repeat
No greedy rule works; this always needs DP
why: Finishing earliest leaves the most room for the rest. Any optimal schedule can swap its first meeting for the earliest-ending one without losing a meeting, so the rule never hurts. That swap idea is the usual way to show a greedy rule is safe.
wrong: An early meeting can run all day and block many short ones.
A short meeting can overlap two others that would both fit without it.
Earliest end time is provably optimal here. DP is needed for variants such as meetings with different values.

q: A thief can carry 10 kg and takes items by best value per kg first. In which version of the problem is this rule guaranteed to give the best total?
options: Always, whether items are whole or can be split
Never: greedy is not guaranteed for any knapsack version
Only when items can be taken in fractions
Either version, as long as items are first sorted by weight
why: In the fractional knapsack, filling by best ratio is optimal, because leftover space is filled with part of the next item. In the 0/1 knapsack, items are whole, so a ratio choice can leave unusable space; that version needs DP.
wrong: With whole items, a high-ratio item can waste space. Items of 6 kg for 30 and two of 5 kg for 20: greedy gets 30, the best is 40.
For the fractional version it is optimal: fill with the best ratio, then take part of the next item.
Input order does not matter, since greedy picks by ratio anyway. What matters is whether items can be split.

q: A DP for climbing stairs fills ways[i] = ways[i - 1] + ways[i - 2] for i up to n. How much memory does it really need?
options: O(1): only the last two values are ever read
O(n): a DP always needs its full table
O(n^2): one row for each step
O(log n): the table can be halved after each step
why: Each value depends only on the previous two, so two variables can roll forward: a, b = b, a + b. Time stays O(n) and extra space drops to O(1). Check which earlier states a step reads before keeping the whole table.
wrong: A table is needed only while older entries are still read. Here each step reads just the last two.
The table is one-dimensional: one number per step, never a grid.
Nothing is halved. The saving comes from dropping values that will never be read again.

q: A memoized function f(i, j) has i from 0 to n - 1 and j from 0 to m - 1. Each new state runs a loop of up to n steps. What is the total time?
options: O(n * m): memoization makes every state cost O(1)
O(2^(n + m)), since it is still recursion
O(n^2 + m): the loop and the states add up
O(n^2 * m): n * m states, each doing O(n) work
why: DP time is the number of states times the work per state. There are n * m states, each computed once thanks to the memo, and each costs up to n steps, so O(n^2 * m). Repeated lookups after that are O(1).
wrong: Memoization means each state is computed once, but computing it still costs its loop of n steps.
Memoization removes the repeated calls, so the work is bounded by the number of states, not exponential.
The loop runs inside every state, so its cost multiplies by the number of states.

q: An array of n numbers never changes, and you must answer 100,000 queries for the sum from index l to index r. Which approach fits best?
options: Loop from l to r for every query
Prefix sums: O(n) setup, then O(1) per query
Sort the array first, then binary search the range
A sliding window that moves from one query to the next
why: With prefix[i] = sum of the first i items, the sum from l to r is prefix[r + 1] - prefix[l]. One O(n) pass of setup, then each query is one subtraction.
wrong: That costs up to O(n) per query, too slow for 100,000 queries on a large array.
Sorting destroys the positions that l and r refer to.
Queries can jump anywhere, so there is no window that moves steadily forward.

q: A sorted array must be checked for two values that add up to a target, in O(n) time and with O(1) extra memory. Which approach fits?
options: Two pointers, one from each end, moving inward
Check every pair with two nested loops
A hash set of the values seen so far
A sliding window of size 2 over neighbouring values
why: If the sum is too small, move the left pointer right; if it is too big, move the right pointer left. Sorting makes each move safe, so each pointer moves at most n times: O(n) time and O(1) memory.
wrong: That uses O(1) memory but O(n^2) time, which misses the O(n) goal.
That is O(n) time but O(n) extra memory, which the requirement rules out.
The two values need not be next to each other, so a window of neighbours misses most pairs.

q: You need the longest stretch of consecutive items with sum at most S. Why does a sliding window work when all values are positive?
options: Sliding windows work the same for any values, positive or not
Positive values let you sort the array first
Adding an item only raises the sum, so shrink from the left
It does not: with positive values you must check all ranges
why: With positive values the sum rises as the window grows and falls as it shrinks. So when the sum passes S, moving the left edge right is the only way back, and no skipped start could do better. Each edge moves at most n times: O(n).
wrong: With negatives, adding an item can lower the sum, so shrinking from the left is no longer the only fix, and the method breaks.
Sorting would break the consecutive requirement, and the window never sorts.
Checking all ranges is the O(n^2) baseline the window improves on. Positive values are exactly what makes the window valid.

q: Prefix sums make range-sum queries O(1). What changes if single values in the array are updated as often as ranges are queried?
options: Nothing: updates are O(1) too, just like queries
Each update can force O(n) prefix values to be rebuilt
Queries become O(log n), but updates stay O(1)
Prefix sums stop giving correct answers once values change
why: prefix[k] includes item i for every k after i, so one update changes up to n prefix values. With frequent updates that is O(n) per update again. Structures such as a Fenwick tree balance both at O(log n).
wrong: Changing item i changes every prefix sum after i, so one update touches up to n entries.
Plain prefix sums keep O(1) queries. It is the updates that get expensive.
If you rebuild after each update the answers stay correct. The cost is the problem.

q: Count the subarrays whose sum is exactly k, where values can be negative. Which technique fits?
options: A sliding window that shrinks when the sum is over k
Two pointers after sorting the array
Binary search on the subarray length
Prefix sums plus a hash map of sums seen so far
why: A subarray from i to j sums to k exactly when prefix[j] - prefix[i] = k. Scanning once and counting how many earlier prefix sums equal current - k, using a hash map, gives O(n), whatever the signs.
wrong: With negative values, shrinking does not reliably lower the sum, so the window can skip valid subarrays.
Sorting scrambles which items are consecutive, so the subarrays are lost.
Whether a length works is not monotonic here, so there is nothing to binary search.
